question: Why must twin-engine aeroplanes be limited in how far they may fly from an adequate aerodrome?

options.text: Twin-engine aeroplanes are not equipped with long range navigation systems
Twin-engine aeroplanes cannot climb above the weather with one engine inoperative
Twin-engine aeroplanes carry less fuel than larger aeroplanes and so cannot hold for very long at all
Losing an engine or a major system is a greater problem than on a three- or four-engine aeroplane

explanation: An engine or major system failure over water or remote areas causes greater problems on a twin than on an aeroplane with three or four engines, so the distance from an adequate aerodrome is limited.

question: Beyond what distance from an adequate aerodrome does a twin-engine public transport flight become an extended range operation?

options.text: One hour's flight time in still air at the normal one-engine-inoperative cruise speed
400 NM measured along the planned track, whatever the cruise speed used
Two hours' flight time in still air at the normal all-engines cruise speed
Thirty minutes' flight time at the one-engine-inoperative cruise speed in the forecast wind

explanation: The limit is one hour's flight time, in still air and standard conditions, at the normal one-engine-inoperative cruise speed.

question: Do the extended twin operations rules apply only to twin jets?

options.text: Yes, only to aeroplanes above 45 360 kg
No, they also apply to all four-engine jets
Yes, only to twin-engine turbojet aeroplanes on public transport flights
No, twin turboprops and piston twins are included too

explanation: The limit applies to all twin-engine aeroplanes, including those powered by turboprops and reciprocating engines.

question: What is the threshold time for extended twin operations?

options.text: 120 minutes
180 minutes
90 minutes
60 minutes

explanation: The threshold time is 60 minutes at the normal one-engine-inoperative cruise speed.

question: What is the threshold distance?

options.text: The distance between the two adequate aerodromes furthest apart on the route
The still air distance flown in 60 minutes at the normal all-engines-operating cruise speed of the type
The still air distance flown in 60 minutes at the normal one-engine-inoperative cruise speed
The distance flown in 120 minutes at the one-engine-inoperative speed in the forecast wind

explanation: Threshold distance is the distance travelled in still air in 60 minutes at the normal one-engine-inoperative cruise speed.

question: A twin's normal one-engine-inoperative cruise speed is 380 kt TAS. What is its threshold distance?

options.text: 760 NM
570 NM
190 NM
380 NM

explanation: Threshold distance is the still air distance in 60 minutes: 380 NM.

question: Up to what maximum diversion time may extended twin operations typically be approved?

options.text: 120 minutes
90 minutes
180 minutes
240 minutes

explanation: An operator may be approved for diversion times up to 180 minutes or less, such as 90, 120 or 138 minutes, at the one-engine-inoperative cruise speed in still air.

question: What is the "rule time"?

options.text: The time needed to descend to FL100 after a loss of pressurisation at cruise level
The maximum time any point on the route may be from a suitable aerodrome, as approved
The time from take-off to the first point on the route that lies beyond the threshold distance
The time spent beyond the threshold distance on the whole of the planned flight

explanation: Rule time is the maximum time that any point on the route may be from a suitable aerodrome for landing, as specified by the authority and included in the operations manual.

question: What is the "rule distance"?

options.text: The distance from the departure aerodrome to the ETOPS entry point
The distance flown in the rule time at the normal all-engines cruise speed in still air
The distance flown in the rule time at the normal one-engine-inoperative cruise speed
The distance flown in 60 minutes at the one-engine-inoperative cruise speed in still air

explanation: Rule distance is the distance travelled in the rule time at the normal one-engine-inoperative cruise speed.

question: A twin is approved for 120 minutes with a one-engine-inoperative cruise speed of 400 kt TAS. What is its rule distance?

options.text: 400 NM
800 NM
480 NM

explanation: 120 minutes at 400 kt is 800 NM in still air.

question: Where does the ETOPS segment of a flight begin?

options.text: At the first point beyond the threshold distance from any adequate aerodrome
At the top of climb after leaving the departure aerodrome on the planned route
At the last point within 400 NM of the departure aerodrome
At the point of equal time between the two en route alternates

explanation: The segment begins at the ETOPS entry point, where the aeroplane is first more than the threshold distance from any adequate aerodrome, and ends at the exit point, where it is last more than that distance.

question: What is the normal one-engine-inoperative cruise speed used for?

options.text: As the speed for the descent after loss of pressurisation
As the planning speed for the whole of the flight
Only to establish the maximum distance from an adequate aerodrome
As the speed to be flown in every case of engine failure, whatever the position

explanation: The operator sets a speed not exceeding VMO, based on the TAS that can be maintained with one engine inoperative. It is only intended for establishing the maximum distance from an adequate aerodrome.

question: Which of these does the authority consider before extending the threshold time?

options.text: The length of the operator's longest route
The number of passengers carried on the route each season
The cost of fuel at the en route alternates
Propulsion system reliability and engine reliability monitoring

explanation: Factors include propulsion system reliability, maintenance programme, dispatch requirements, training, operations limitations, validation flights, continuing surveillance and engine reliability monitoring.

question: What makes an aerodrome "adequate" for extended twin operations?

options.text: Fuel available at the price agreed with the operator and customs available at all hours
Weather forecast at or above planning minima from one hour before to one hour after landing
Long enough runways and the necessary services, with at least one instrument let-down aid
Location within 60 minutes of the planned route at the all-engines cruise speed

explanation: An adequate aerodrome has long enough runways and is equipped with ATC, lighting, communications, weather reporting, navaids, safety cover and at least one let-down aid for an instrument approach.

question: Which of these qualifies as the let-down aid needed at an adequate aerodrome?

options.text: A windsock
An ATIS broadcast
Ground radar
A VOLMET station

explanation: At least one let-down aid for an instrument approach must be available, and ground radar qualifies.

question: Who decides on the day that an adequate aerodrome is also suitable?

options.text: The commander, using the operator's criteria
The authority, when granting the approval
The air traffic control centre for the area
The maintenance department, before the aircraft is dispatched

explanation: The commander must be satisfied on the day, using the operator's criteria, that enough adequate aerodromes are suitable, taking into account weather and equipment unserviceabilities.

question: For what period must the weather at an ETOPS en route alternate be at or above planning minima?

options.text: From one hour before to one hour after the estimated time of passing abeam the aerodrome
From the earliest expected landing time until one hour after the latest possible landing
For the whole period of validity of the aerodrome forecast issued before departure
From the time of departure until the aircraft has landed at the destination

explanation: An aerodrome may be selected only when reports or forecasts show conditions at or above planning minima between the anticipated time of landing and one hour after the latest possible time of landing.

question: What must an operator make sure of before an extended twin operation?

options.text: The destination has two separate runways, each with an instrument approach available
A suitable en route alternate is available within the approved diversion time
The route is entirely within VHF radio range of land stations
Both engines have been changed within the last 1000 hours of flight

explanation: Before an ETOPS flight the operator must ensure that a suitable ETOPS en route alternate is available within the appropriate diversion time.

question: How is the minimum equipment list affected by extended twin operations?

options.text: It applies only to the cabin and passenger equipment
It allows more items of equipment to be inoperative on departure than normal
It is replaced by the master list of the manufacturer
It reflects the higher redundancy needed in primary systems

explanation: Primary system redundancy levels appropriate to ETOPS are reflected in the MEL, which is re-evaluated and adjusted for aircraft already in service.

question: What is a primary airframe system in this context?

options.text: Any system that is used during every single phase of the flight, from engine start to shutdown
A system with fundamental influence on safety that could be affected by an engine shutdown
Any system whose failure would be shown by a master caution light
A system that can be replaced by the crew in flight without special tools

explanation: Primary airframe systems have a fundamental influence on flight safety and could be adversely affected by the shutdown of a power unit, such as electrics, hydraulics, pneumatics, fuel and flight controls.

question: Which of these is listed as a primary airframe system for extended twin operations?

options.text: Cargo fire suppression
Galley ovens
In-flight entertainment
Cabin reading lights

explanation: Examples include electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic, flight instruments, fuel, flight controls, ice protection, engine start and ignition, navigation and communications, APU, air conditioning and pressurisation, cargo fire suppression and fire detection.

question: What communication facilities are needed before dispatch on an extended twin operation?

options.text: HF data link to the operator's base along the whole of the route
Satellite telephone contact with each en route alternate
Reliable two-way voice with ATC at the one-engine-inoperative cruise altitudes
VHF coverage of the whole route at the planned all-engines cruise level and on the diversions

explanation: Communication facilities must give reliable two-way voice with the appropriate ATC unit under all expected propagation conditions at the one-engine-inoperative cruise altitudes, on the route and to alternates.

question: What navigation facilities are needed before dispatch on an extended twin operation?

options.text: An NDB at each point where the aircraft passes the threshold distance
Visual aids only at each alternate, as the route is flown by inertial navigation
VOR/DME coverage of the whole route at the planned all-engines cruise level
Non-visual aids giving the required accuracy on the route and to the alternates

explanation: Non-visual ground aids must give, with the aircraft's equipment, the accuracy required over the route and the diversion routes, and approved visual and non-visual aids must be available at the alternates.

question: What is the "critical fuel" for extended twin operations?

options.text: The fuel needed at the destination to hold for 30 minutes at 1500 ft
The fuel needed to fly the whole route at the one-engine-inoperative speed
The fuel from the most critical point to the diversion aerodrome after a failure
The fuel from the departure aerodrome to the ETOPS entry point at the planned cruise level

explanation: Critical fuel is the fuel from the most critical point (or equal time point) to the diversion aerodrome, based on the worst of the failure cases.

question: Which failure is the worst case for extended twin critical fuel?

options.text: Total pressurisation failure with both engines running
Simultaneous failure of an engine and the pressurisation
Loss of one generator and one hydraulic system
Failure of an engine with the pressurisation still working

explanation: Simultaneous engine and pressurisation failure is the worst scenario: emergency descent to FL100 and cruise there on one engine, at high fuel flow.

question: After a total pressurisation failure on an extended twin operation, what profile is assumed for critical fuel?

options.text: Emergency descent to FL100 at VMO/MMO with speed brakes, then LRC to the diversion
Drift-down to the one-engine stabilising level, then cruise at the selected speed
Descent to FL250 at normal descent speed, then cruise at Mach 0.74 to the diversion aerodrome
Continued cruise at the planned level with oxygen until reaching the destination

explanation: The aircraft makes an emergency descent to FL100 at VMO/MMO with speed brakes extended, then cruises to the diversion at LRC speed.

question: After an engine failure only (pressurisation working) on an extended twin operation, what profile is assumed?

options.text: Continued cruise at the planned level and speed
Immediate descent to 1500 ft and hold
Descent and cruise at the selected speeds and stabilising level
Emergency descent to FL100 at VMO/MMO with the speed brakes extended

explanation: With only an engine failure the aircraft descends and cruises at the selected speeds and stabilising level.

question: How is the critical fuel used at dispatch?

options.text: It is compared with the planned fuel at the critical point, and more is loaded if it is greater
It is used only in flight, to decide whether to continue past the critical point
It replaces the alternate fuel, as no destination alternate is ever needed on such flights
It is added to the trip fuel and contingency in every case, whether or not it is needed

explanation: The greatest of the all-engine and single-engine cases is compared with the fuel planned to be on board at the critical point; if it is greater, additional fuel must be uplifted.

question: Which assumptions are common to the critical fuel reserve graphs of the planning jet?

options.text: Drift-down to the stabilising level, 30 minutes' hold and a 10% allowance for errors in the wind forecast
Cruise at the planned level, a direct approach and landing, with no allowance for wind
Descent to 1500 ft over the alternate, 45 minutes' hold and two missed approaches
Emergency descent and cruise at 10 000 ft, 15 minutes' hold, a missed approach and 5% for wind errors

explanation: Both graphs assume pressurisation failure, emergency descent to and cruise at 10 000 ft, 250 KIAS descent to 1500 ft, 15 minutes' hold, one missed approach, approach and landing, and a 5% wind error allowance.

question: Why does the planning jet's one-engine-inoperative critical fuel graph include APU fuel?

options.text: The APU must run throughout every flight segment beyond the threshold distance from land
The APU is used to restart the failed engine after the descent to FL100
The APU must run to replace part of the lost electrical and pneumatic supply
The APU supplies thrust to help hold altitude on one engine

explanation: With an engine and pressurisation failure the APU is started in flight to provide, in part, the essential electrics and pneumatics lost with the engine.

question: For which conditions are corrections given beneath the planning jet's critical fuel reserve graphs?

options.text: Headwinds above 100 kt and rain
Night flying and low visibility
Temperatures above ISA and icing
Weights above MLM and turbulence

explanation: Corrections are given for temperatures hotter than ISA and for icing conditions.

question: The critical fuel graph gives 8000 kg for an engine and pressurisation failure. The temperature at FL100 is ISA +10°C (0.5% per 10°C) and icing is forecast (20%). What is the corrected critical fuel?
explanation: 8000 × 1.005 = 8040 kg for temperature, then × 1.20 for icing = 9648 kg.

question: How is the critical point between two en route alternates found in still air?

options.text: Where the track is closest to the nearer of the two alternates
Where the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them cuts the track
Where a line joining the two alternates crosses the track
At the mid-point of the track between the ETOPS entry point and the ETOPS exit point

explanation: In still air the points equidistant from the two alternates lie on the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them; where it cuts the track is the still air critical point.

question: How is the critical point line corrected for wind?

options.text: Apply the wind to the all-engines TAS and recompute the point of equal time for the route
Plot the wind vector for the still air diversion time and draw a parallel line through its end
Rotate the still air critical line by the drift angle on the diversion and read off the new crossing point
Move the point along track by the wind component times the flight time to the critical point

explanation: Find the still air time to either alternate, multiply it by the wind speed to get a wind vector, plot it back from the still air point, and draw the equal time line parallel to the critical line through its end.

question: The still air critical point is 690 NM from each alternate. The one-engine-inoperative TAS is 400 kt and the wind speed 85 kt. How long is the wind vector to be plotted?

options.text: 173 NM
147 NM
85 NM
117 NM

explanation: Still air time = 690/400 = 103.5 min. Wind vector = 85 × 103.5/60 = 147 NM.

question: The still air critical point is 630 NM from each alternate. The one-engine-inoperative TAS is 420 kt and the wind speed 60 kt. How long is the wind vector?

options.text: 105 NM
60 NM
75 NM
90 NM

explanation: Still air time = 630/420 = 1.5 h. Wind vector = 60 × 1.5 = 90 NM.

question: Which en route alternates are used to find the most critical point for the critical fuel?

options.text: The alternate nearest the destination and the departure
Any two alternates chosen by the commander on the day
The two alternates furthest along the track
The two alternates nearest the departure aerodrome

explanation: The most critical point is the one based on the two alternates furthest along the track, as more fuel has been used by then.

question: What must be true of the planned fuel at the critical point?

options.text: It must be at least the critical fuel to either alternate
It must equal the trip fuel to the destination
It must be at least twice the final reserve fuel for the destination
It must equal half of the take-off fuel

explanation: The flight-planned fuel at the critical point must be equal to or greater than the critical fuel to either alternate; if not, extra fuel is loaded.

question: What is the area of operation for extended twin operations?

options.text: The area covered by the operator's VHF radio network
The airspace within 60 minutes' flying time of the departure aerodrome at cruise speed
The airspace above FL290 along the oceanic tracks
The region in which the operator is authorised to conduct such flights

explanation: The area of operation is the region within which the operator is authorised to conduct ETOPS, defined by the approved diversion time at single-engine cruise speed in still air and ISA.

question: With which values is the planning jet's area of operation (diversion distance) chart entered?

options.text: Speed schedule and weight at the point of diversion, then the approved time
Pressure altitude and the estimated landing weight at the alternate aerodrome
Wind component and temperature at the point of diversion
Fuel remaining and distance to the destination

explanation: Enter with the speed and the weight at the point of diversion, select the approved time and read the maximum diversion distance. Still air and ISA are assumed.

question: What does the planning jet's one-engine-inoperative in-flight diversion graph assume?

options.text: One engine inoperative, no pressurisation failure, drift-down to the selected cruise level
One engine inoperative and pressurisation failure, with the cruise flown at 10 000 ft
Both engines operating, normal cruise at the planned level to the alternate
Both engines operating, pressurisation failure and descent to 10 000 ft

explanation: The graph gives fuel and time from the diversion point to the alternate with one engine inoperative and no pressurisation failure, drifting down to cruise at the selected level.

question: On the planning jet's one-engine-inoperative diversion graph, the solid pressure altitude line is 6000 ft and the dashed line 26 000 ft. What must be done for a cruise at FL160?

options.text: Add the values from both lines together
Use the solid line, as it is the lower one
Interpolate halfway between the two lines
Use the dashed line, as it is more limiting

explanation: FL160 lies halfway between 6000 ft and 26 000 ft, so interpolate halfway between the two lines.

question: What do the planning jet's gear-down ferry flight data assume?

options.text: All engines at long range cruise, climb excluded
All engines operating at 220 KIAS, with climb and descent included
One engine inoperative at 220 KIAS, cruise only, climb and descent not included
All engines at 250 KIAS below FL100 only

explanation: The gear-down ferry data are for all engines operating at 220 KIAS, and include climb and descent fuel and time.

question: What is fuel tankering?

options.text: Carrying extra fuel so that the alternate can be further from the destination
Carrying more fuel than needed because it is cheaper at the departure aerodrome
Uplifting fuel at an en route stop so the next sector can be flown non-stop
Transferring fuel between tanks in flight to keep the centre of gravity in limits

explanation: When fuel costs more at the destination, carrying extra from departure may be economical; much of it is then used on the return or next sector.

question: Why does tankered fuel not all arrive at the destination?

options.text: It evaporates at high altitude in the tanks
Part of it is burnt carrying the extra weight
It is used to cool the engine oil in the cruise
It is dumped before landing to reduce weight

explanation: The higher gross weight increases fuel consumption, so a smaller but significant percentage of the tankered fuel is burnt on the way.

question: With which values is the planning jet's tankering graph entered?

options.text: Trip distance in NGM, take-off weight with tankered fuel and the departure fuel price
Cruise Mach number, zero fuel weight and the destination fuel price
Flight time, average wind component and the fuel prices at both aerodromes
Trip distance in NAM, cruise pressure altitude and landing weight without tankered fuel

explanation: The graph is entered with trip air distance, cruise pressure altitude and landing weight without tankering, and gives the percentage of the surplus fuel that will be burnt.

question: When should the tankering graphs not be used?

options.text: When the trip is shorter than 1000 NAM in still air conditions
When the wind component is a tailwind
When tankering would reduce the cruise altitude capability
When the destination has no alternate

explanation: The charts should only be used if the cruise altitude capability is not adversely affected by tankering.

question: When is tankering economical?

options.text: When the destination fuel price is greater than the break-even price
When the trip distance is less than 500 NAM in still air
When the surplus fuel burn is more than 20% of the extra fuel
When the departure fuel price is greater than the price at the destination aerodrome

explanation: The fuel price graph gives the break-even destination price for the surplus burn percentage and departure price. Tankering pays only if the destination price exceeds it.

question: A jet tankers 2000 kg of extra fuel. The tankering graph shows that 10% of it will be burnt. How much of the extra fuel reaches the destination?
explanation: 10% of 2000 kg, 200 kg, is burnt carrying it, so 1800 kg arrives.

question: 10% of tankered fuel will be burnt on a sector. Fuel at departure costs 90 cents per US gallon. Roughly what is the break-even price at the destination?

options.text: 100 cents
99 cents
90 cents
81 cents

explanation: Only 90% of the fuel bought arrives, so each arriving gallon costs 90/0.9 = 100 cents. Tankering pays if destination fuel costs more than that.

question: For the tankering graph, a trip of 1600 NGM is flown at 480 kt TAS with a 30 kt headwind. What trip distance is entered?

options.text: 1707 NAM
1500 NAM
1650 NAM
1600 NAM

explanation: The graph uses air distance. GS = 450 kt, so NAM = 1600 × 480/450 = 1707.

question: Which of these is typically held in a computer flight planning database?

options.text: The catering order for each sector
The operator's fuel policy and the aircraft's performance data
The passengers' names and seat numbers for the sector
The crew's licence and medical expiry dates

explanation: The database holds navigation data, meteorological data, standard routes, ATC routes and oceanic tracks, fuel policy, aircraft limits and performance, aerodrome data, preferred alternates, fuel costs and the preferred cruise method.

question: Which minimum information does a computer flight planning system usually need to produce a plan?

options.text: The full route with all its waypoints, winds and temperatures entered by hand
Aircraft registration, crew names, the fuel price and the passenger list
Only the departure and destination, as everything else is chosen automatically
Aircraft type, departure and destination, cruise mode, traffic load and block time

explanation: Most systems need at least the aircraft type, departure and destination, cruise mode, traffic load and block time. Errors in what is loaded give wrong plans: garbage in, garbage out.

question: On a computer flight plan, what does "MXSH 5/KOK" indicate?

options.text: Maximum wind shear of 5 kt per 1000 ft at that point, so clear air turbulence is possible
The fifth waypoint on the route, where the maximum cruise level can be reached
Maximum safe height of 5000 ft at that point, so the minimum altitude must be observed
A maximum of 5 minutes' holding expected at that point before the descent begins

explanation: MXSH is the maximum wind shear, here 5 kt per 1000 ft at that waypoint. Shear of this strength makes clear air turbulence possible and a level change might give better economy.

question: On a computer flight plan, the wind is given as "27045". What does it mean?

options.text: 270° magnetic at 45 kt
270° true at 45 kt
270° true at 4.5 kt
027° true at 045 kt

explanation: The five-figure group gives direction in tens of degrees true (27 = 270°) and speed in knots (045 = 45 kt).

question: On a computer flight plan, what is "MTR"?

options.text: The mean true range
The magnetic track
The mean temperature
The minimum terrain reading

explanation: MTR is the magnetic track; DFT is drift, ZD the zone (leg) distance and ZT the zone time.

question: On a computer flight plan, what is "DSTR"?

options.text: The distance flown so far
The descent rate required
The distance to the next waypoint
The total distance remaining

explanation: DSTR is total distance remaining; ZD is the leg distance.

question: On a computer flight plan, what does "CT" show?

options.text: The contingency time
The accumulated flight time
The cruise temperature
The compass track to the next waypoint

explanation: CT is the cumulative flight time; ZT is the time for the individual leg.

question: On a computer flight plan, what is "CON 000155 00/03"?

options.text: 155 kg of fuel consumed in the climb, taking 3 minutes
155 NM to the first waypoint, reached after 3 minutes
155 kg of contingency fuel, equal to 3 minutes of flight
155 kg of fuel for holding over the destination for 3 minutes

explanation: CON is contingency fuel, here 155 kg (5% of a 3091 kg route fuel), equivalent to 3 minutes' flying.

question: On a computer flight plan, what does the "OPNLWT" (operational weight) figure represent?

options.text: The aircraft weight less fuel and payload
The maximum weight for the operation
The aircraft weight with fuel but no payload
The landing weight at the destination

explanation: The operational weight is the weight less fuel and payload, effectively the dry operating weight for the flight.

question: A route of 362 NGM takes 55 minutes with an average wind component of 29 kt tail. What is the air distance, as shown on the plan?

options.text: 389 NAM
362 NAM
333 NAM
335 NAM

question: A leg is 400 NGM, flown in 50 minutes with a 30 kt headwind component. What air distance is flown?

options.text: 400 NAM
375 NAM
430 NAM
425 NAM

explanation: With a headwind the air distance is greater: 400 + (30 × 50/60) = 425 NAM.

question: Which items in the flight plan part of a computer printout are not transmitted unless the aircraft becomes overdue?

options.text: Endurance, persons on board and emergency and survival equipment
Cruising speed, first cruising level and route
Aircraft identification, type and wake turbulence category
Departure aerodrome, off-blocks time and destination with its alternate

explanation: The supplementary information, such as fuel endurance, persons on board, emergency radio, survival equipment, dinghies and aircraft colours, is held and passed only if needed for search and rescue.

question: Which of these should a pilot check on a computer flight plan?

options.text: That the winds and average wind component tally with the forecast
That the route has the fewest possible waypoints
That the take-off weight is exactly the maximum take-off mass of the type
That the plan was printed on the operator's headed paper

explanation: Check that the plan is up to date and uses the latest forecasts, that fuel and times make sense for the season, that tracks and distances are sensible, that winds tally with the forecast, that alternates are acceptable and the cruise method is right.

question: How can a computer flight plan for a new or rarely flown route be checked?

options.text: It cannot be checked and must be accepted as printed
With the aircraft's simplified planning data or agreed rules of thumb
By asking the air traffic control centre to confirm the fuel
By comparing it with the computer plan printed for the reverse direction

explanation: For a new or rarely flown route, the plan can be verified with the simplified flight planning data or agreed rules of thumb based on average fuel flows and speeds.

question: Can a computer flight plan allow for forecast bad weather in calculating the fuel required?

options.text: Only for flights that stay within a single FIR from departure to arrival
Yes, using the forecast winds and temperatures loaded from the meteorological office
Only if the pilot enters every forecast wind by hand before printing
No, computer plans always assume still air and ISA for every flight

explanation: Computer plans use the forecast meteorological data automatically loaded into the system, so winds and temperatures are taken into account; extra fuel for other weather is added according to policy.

question: After an in-flight re-routing, does the computer automatically produce a new flight plan for the crew?

options.text: Yes, but only on oceanic routes
Yes, it is sent to the aircraft at once
No, the crew replan with the FMS or the manuals
Only if the delay exceeds 30 minutes

explanation: The ground computer produces plans before flight and can often file the ATC flight plan; an in-flight re-route does not automatically generate a new plan, so the crew replan using the FMS or manuals.
